speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43, I request unanimous consent of the House to discuss an important and urgent matter that affects all Canadians.
Since the price of milk has increased dramatically recently, more specifically six times in 14 months, since

milk is an essential food for children, and since a family that consumes four quarts of milk daily spends over $250 annually because of the unduly high price of milk, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert):
That this House study the means to roll back the price of milk and other essential foods to a more acceptable level, in order to allow all Canadians, regardless of their income, to have access to those food products that are essential to a balanced diet, and this through reinstating the subsidies on whole milk.

PROPOSED GUARANTEED ANNUAL INCOME AND RETAIL
subsubtopic: DISCOUNTS-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of pressing and urgent necessity.
Considering that the 1.3 per cent decline in our Gross National Product over the last three months of 1974 is certainly the worst recorded since 1960-61, and considering that any such decline reflects a falling off of our productive capacity, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette):
That this House look into the possibility of setting up a guaranteed annual income scheme for all Canadians, as well as a consumer price compensated discount program, as incentives to the lagging Canadian economy, as evidenced by the most recent GNP figures, and to prevent the battle against inflation from being fought at the expense of small Canadian taxpayers.

Parliamentary government requires that ministers be accountable in principle for the actions of their deputy and assistant deputy ministers (under-secretaries and assistant under-secretaries), as for all public servants, in relation to the discharge of their official responsibilities without removing from such persons their personal accountability for their actions. speechtext:
1. 2.	Is the objective of the Corporation to develop Canadian-controlled and Canadian-managed corporations and operate profitably and in the best interests of the shareholder and, if so, on what policy basis has almost 90 per cent of all cash invested so far by the Corporation been utilized to acquire shares of, or interests in, foreign corporations and businesses?

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: GOVERNMENT INVESTMENT IN CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer to this question is somewhat lengthy. I have provided a copy to the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) and I wonder if it could be taken as read.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT INVESTMENT IN CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
speechtext: Is that agreed?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT INVESTMENT IN CANADA DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION
speechtext:
Agreed.
[Editor's Note: The answer is as follows:]
1.	The government has purchased $250 million of common shares of the Canada Development Corporation for cash and has also sold to the CDC the former Polymer Corporation Limited for CDC common shares. These common shares entitle the government to receive any dividend declared by the corporation. The declaration of dividends is the responsibility of the CDC board of directors. The board has not yet considered it advantageous to declare a dividend. The government appreciates and shares the view of the CDC board that at this early stage in the life of the corporation it has been beneficial to both the CDC and the government as a shareholder to keep the earnings invested in the corporation. Two senior government officials are ex officio members of the CDC board of directors and the Minister of Finance currently elects the balance of the board of directors at the annual shareholders meeting. This enables the government to effectively monitor the management and the performance of the corporation.
2.	Pursuant to the CDC Act, the corporation's objectives are to help develop and maintain strong Canadian-controlled and Canadian-managed corporations in the private sector of the economy, and to operate in anticipation of

profits and in the best interests of shareholders. I think that the CDC's resources have effectively been used in order to achieve these objectives. The purchase of a 30% interest in Texasgulf incorporated at a cost of 271 million dollars to this time represents the CDC's major cash investment. Although incorporated in the United States Texasgulf donives about two thirds of its revenue from Canadian operations and is planning major additional investments in Canada which will develop Canadian natural resources. Through Polysar, which was acquired by means of an exchange of shares rather than for cash, the CDC is further investing substantial amounts of funds to build a Canadian petrochemical plant which will be comparable in size to the larger ethylene producing plants in the world. This new petrochemical complex represents an investment in excess of 400 million dollars. The establishment of Connlab Holdings Limited in which the CDC has already invested 35 million dollars represents an attempt to create a major Canadian controlled and managed company in the health care field. The CDC has also invested over 10 million dollars in three Canadian venture capital firms, helping to create two of those in Vancouver and Montreal. The corporation is also a partner in the group planning the development of the Mackenzie Delta gas pipeline. From the preceding it is clear that the CDC's investments have been undertaken in furtherance of its major objectives.
3. The CDC's head office has been established in Vancouver. The full time operating officers or staff amount to seven in the Vancouver head office and seventeen in the other operating office in Toronto.

1.	As a general rule, do government employees, when travelling on official business at public expense, travel in first-class accommodation

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (President of Treasury Board):
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVANTS-TRAVEL EXPENSES ON OFFICIAL BUSINESS
speechtext:
1.
Government employees on official business generally travel economy air and, for one way rail trips of four hours or less, coach class.
2. Exceptions to the general rule are: Paragraph 2.03 of the Treasury Board Travel Directive, "... A higher standard of accommodation may be authorized only when, in the opinion of the employer, the extra cost is justified by program-related reasons, such as: (a) when no less expensive accommodation is available and a delay in arrival is not acceptable, or (b) when travel is within a country or between countries when economy class air travel present health hazards or discomfort to the employee, or (c) when in exceptional circumstances, such as for reasons of protocol, an employee officially accompanies another person travelling first class." Paragraph 2.09 of the Treasury Board Travel Directive referring to rail travel in excess of four hours, " ... For longer trips a higher standard shall be authorized with Canadian roomette or equivalent accommodation being provided for overnight travel." A deputy minister may authorize first class travel if in his opinion it is appropriate to do so.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: OIL-CONFERENCE OF PRODUCING, CONSUMING AND THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES-REASON FOR FAILURE OF CANADA TO ATTEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Prime Minister concerning the very important conference on oil called by France for April 7 I believe, involving some ten countries including France, representatives of the producing countries, representatives of the consuming countries, and representatives of the third world, a conference to which Canada has not been invited. I should like to ask the Acting Prime Minister whether the Government of Canada approves of this conference or disapproves of it and whether it accepts the fact that it has not been invited or whether it has protested its not being invited.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-CONFERENCE OF PRODUCING, CONSUMING AND THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES-REASON FOR FAILURE OF CANADA TO ATTEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps I might respond on behalf of the Acting Prime Minister. For some time Canada has favoured in general terms a meeting between both the producing and consuming countries as well as the developing countries and has sought to participate in the preparatory meetings which will be taking place in Paris in the near future. The position that was taken by the various parties to the international energy agency and indeed by the Government of France, was that the conference should be confined to a limited number of participants in all three categories. The Government of Canada would have preferred to have participated in the preparatory meeting but I think that with Canada and all other countries participating it would have been of such a scale that would have perhaps hindered the making of effective arrangements in the preparatory meeting. We agreed on that basis not to participate.

subtopic: OIL-CONFERENCE OF PRODUCING, CONSUMING AND THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES-CANADIAN POSITION ON SUBJECTS TO BE DISCUSSED AND THROUGH WHOM ADVANCED

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: OIL-CONFERENCE OF PRODUCING, CONSUMING AND THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES-CANADIAN POSITION ON SUBJECTS TO BE DISCUSSED AND THROUGH WHOM ADVANCED
speechtext: I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Due to the fact that this conference, if it is successful along the lines that the Government of France, which is calling this conference, may lay down some very important guidelines for the future relating, for example, to the concept at least of negotiated prices between the producing and consuming countries-a negotiated world price-and the possibility of agreements in principle on a floor price or even the range of level of that floor price, does the Government of Canada have a position on these matters and if so how is this position to be put before this conference?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-CONFERENCE OF PRODUCING, CONSUMING AND THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES-CANADIAN POSITION ON SUBJECTS TO BE DISCUSSED AND THROUGH WHOM ADVANCED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I remind the Leader of the Opposition that this conference, of course, is preparatory to a full conference which will be taking place later this year on the assumption that the preparatory meeting is successful. The government of Canada will be keeping in close touch with these discussions and with the partici-

pants at the conference of the international energy agency, and of course we will be making our views known with regard to the various items which the hon. gentleman has mentioned. The International Energy Agency meeting will take place in the agency on March 6 and 7, that is to say this week. At that time we will be discussing the question of the floor price, among others. We have not taken a final position with regard to the various comments put forward until the propositions are better defined, although we recognize that the floor price could be of significance to Canada with the relatively high cost petroleum resources in the future, and on that basis we will be pursuing the floor price discussion, bearing in mind our interest over the long run in maintaining protection of our own industry.

subtopic: OIL-CONFERENCE OF PRODUCING, CONSUMING AND THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES-CANADIAN POSITION ON SUBJECTS TO BE DISCUSSED AND THROUGH WHOM ADVANCED
speechtext: It is my understanding that if the international agency is present at the conference, it will be present only with observer status. I am asking the Acting Prime Minister or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, if the Government of Canada has views to be expressed at this conference, through whom does it propose to express these views, through Mr. Kissinger?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-CONFERENCE OF PRODUCING, CONSUMING AND THIRD WORLD COUNTRIES-CANADIAN POSITION ON SUBJECTS TO BE DISCUSSED AND THROUGH WHOM ADVANCED
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, obviously the views of the Government of Canada will be made known to all participants with whom we have diplomatic relations, but in particular with the members of the international energy agency who will be participating. In no sense will Canada be bound by the results of the preparatory meeting, and of course we reserve the full right to express our views at the plenary conference when it is held, whether or not we are in agreement with the preparatory meeting.

LENGTH OF TIME BEFORE INTRODUCTION OF MEASURES TO STIMULATE GROWTH-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS ALLOCATED TO HOUSING
speechtext: I have a question for the Minister of Finance. Considering the decline in the real growth of the economy which we have experienced in the last few years, as documented by figures released by Statistics Canada, which also relate to the forecasts that the real growth in the Canadian economy is likely to be in the neighbourhood of just one per cent for 1975, I would like to ask the minister, in light of this information and in light of his own acknowledgement three or four weeks ago that his own forecast made in the budget of last fall needed revision, how long he intends us to wait before he will bring forth these new measures to deal with the Canadian economy which the revelation of these facts fully justifies.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: LENGTH OF TIME BEFORE INTRODUCTION OF MEASURES TO STIMULATE GROWTH-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS ALLOCATED TO HOUSING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that will have to remain a question of judgment. The House should put the situation in perspective. The three month period-and I gather it was a three month period to which the hon. member was referring-was already evident to the government at the time I brought down the budget on November 18. The stimulus injected into the economy at that time, which was in the realm of $3 billion cash deficit, primarily by way of tax reductions, is already being felt by the economy as of January 1 in the form of tax reductions for the 1974 and 1975 taxation years, and when the bill which the House passed last week is passed by the other place, further refunds will be in the hands of Canadian taxpayers.
I would like to say to the hon. member as well that since this stimulus is already injected, since capital investment in plant and equipment is holding up reasonably well, and since, as against the figure of 3.7 per cent real growth for the economy in 1974 we had a figure of 6.8 per cent in real domestic product, that the economy in domestic terms fell off only marginally from the 8.3 of real domestic product in the year before. What really happened in our economy was a drag from our exports, a falling off of our exports caused by a stagnant recessionary American economy, a stagnant Japanese economy and a flat European economy.

subtopic: LENGTH OF TIME BEFORE INTRODUCTION OF MEASURES TO STIMULATE GROWTH-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS ALLOCATED TO HOUSING
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: LENGTH OF TIME BEFORE INTRODUCTION OF MEASURES TO STIMULATE GROWTH-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS ALLOCATED TO HOUSING
speechtext: It is for those reasons that I am examining the situation in the United States, in Europe and in Japan because they are crucial to our exports. I am also examining the effect of the stimulus already in the enonomy.

subtopic: LENGTH OF TIME BEFORE INTRODUCTION OF MEASURES TO STIMULATE GROWTH-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS ALLOCATED TO HOUSING
speechtext: A good part of the statistics revealed by Statistics Canada flatly contradicts what the minister has said or argued and specifically I refer to their singling out of the 10.4 per cent drop in residential construction which has nothing to do with foreign export sales. With the 10.4 per cent drop in residential construction in 1974 being one of the major reasons for the decline in growth of our GNP, I would like to ask the minister if the government has any intention of bolstering the housing market to provide houses which are needed, and to provide jobs, by injecting a large amount of money soon into the construction of new housing.

subtopic: LENGTH OF TIME BEFORE INTRODUCTION OF MEASURES TO STIMULATE GROWTH-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN FUNDS ALLOCATED TO HOUSING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is perfectly right that a major factor in the slow growth was a sharp drop in real consumer demand in housing and in some durable goods. One of the priorities in the budget was a further allocation of funds to give some leverage to my colleague the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. The fact remains that in analysing the figures for 1974 which have just come in, the difference between 6.8 per cent for real domestic product and 3.7 per cent for the total real growth in the economy or the gross national product is represented by the drag on our economy of falling exports.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have heard an awful lot about food production and guaranteeing producers of food some kind of security, particularly when we ask them to go all-out on production. Whether or not we have a constant supply of domestically produced food in Canada in the coming years is not totally in the hands of the farmers whom we have asked to go all-out on production. Even though our farmers are the top food producers in the world, it takes more than that to be sure we have this kind of production. Farmers also need legislation that will give them the guarantees they need in order to continue producing. Their basic need is a floor price that will protect them against low prices that will ruin them overnight. If we ask them to produce without giving them any kind of security, they will go down the drain.
I was asked earlier in the House whether I had met with the ministers of agriculture for Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick concerning a problem those provinces face today. This problem, which has existed for some weeks, concerns the disastrous prices they are receiving for potatoes in those areas and in other areas of Canada. The price of potatoes has gone down drastically. There is no denying the fact that the provinces of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island depend to a great extent on returns from potato crops to support their economies. With present prices, these provinces will receive for their potato crops this year less than half of what they received last year; and the situation may become even worse. In any event, the prices received at the present time are disastrous.
Some people think that low prices are beneficial and that producers should go all-out on production, giving away the product in order to offset inflation. All one has to do is check what has happened in the past to find out that this is not so. What happens is that you have a tremendous glut or overproduction, with tremendously depressed prices. This is followed by a shortage of production and an increase in price. So there really is no benefit to the producer and no benefit to the consumer.

March 5, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
We have stabilization legislation on the books at the present time and it did the job in its day. However, today this legislation falls short of being the sort of over-all legislation the farmers need. It is outdated. A guaranteed floor price is required to keep the farmers producing enough of certain commodities to fill the demand, and if we want a strong farm economy in the future we must give the farmers the kind of legislation they need. Statistics Canada has indicated that net farm income is expected to nose-dive by 12 per cent in 1975.1 would like to know what other parts of society are being asked to accept such a nose-dive in 1975. Many segments of our society are refusing reasonable offers such as a 25 per cent increase.
Farm input costs have gone up by more than 25 points over the increase in consumer costs during the same period. Statistics indicate that many of those who are producing these important commodities in Canada have not received an increase in income comparable to increases received by people in other parts of society and in other segments of agriculture. I have in mind at the present time the potato growers to whom I have referred. Having regard to the potato growers, let me read a telex which I received from the Quebec minister of agriculture. He said:
Further to my telex regarding low prices obtained by Quebec potato producers and disastrous situation which may follow with regard to spring sowing, I would like to know immediately if you are planning a special program within the framework of a stabilization bill or other to assure stability of income for our potato producers thus permitting them to be more optimistic about their future.
I might add that the Canadian Horticultural Council is also concerned about this situation. This situation, coupled with other uncertainties that face our farmers, is prompting many farmers to pick up the phone and cancel fertilizer orders, or to call a real estate agent to see if they can get out while the getting is good. Faced with these uncertainties, we cannot have all-out food production. It is legislation of this kind which will prompt farmers to decide not to sell-out but to keep on producing.
Legislation already on the books gives farmers a deficiency payment if the market price in any one year is less than 80 per cent of the average price of the ten preceding years. Nine commodities were automatically covered, but the number of commodities covered by the new bill is somewhat greater. This bill calls for a series of important changes. The first and most important is that farmers will be guaranteed an average of 90 per cent of the average market value, up from 80 per cent. The base period would be the last five years instead of the last ten.
One of the real weaknesses in the old act was that rapid increases in farm input costs could put the guaranteed support levels so far below the cost of production that the legislation would become a farce. This is exactly what did happen in the last two years. We want stabilization legislation to do its job; that is why this bill calls for indexing the support levels to reflect production costs. In this way our legislation will be able to cope with any quick swings in the marketplace. Some people say that is not good planning. I would ask them how they expect, in a world trading pattern, and so on, to do things in any other fashion.

The amendments go even further. They allow for stabilization programs to be set up for products which are produced and sold in a specific region. This will make the legislation much more valuable for commodities such as potatoes and tobacco. We have already spoken about potatoes. When we talk about potatoes, we think of the area of Canada which produces potatoes, commonly known as eastern Canada, with the hope that we can regionalize it. I do not think in this case it would be satisfactory to have a region such as Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick alone. Quebec and Ontario, I believe, should be part of that region. Those provinces produce potatoes, although they do not produce sufficient for their own consumption and import from the maritime provinces.
Anything that can be done to improve the price of potatoes in the maritimes would necessarily be affected by what the market for that commodity is in Quebec or in Ontario. They are all Canadian producers, producing the same commodity for the market. Their costs are similar regardless which province is concerned. Under the new legislation, a region could be that part of eastern Canada which produces potatoes that are consumed mostly in that area. Of the total amount of potatoes we produce, we export only about 6 per cent and many of these are used for seed. The amendments also provide for top-loading. By this I mean that provincial governments and/or producers can increase the stabilization base higher than 90 per cent if they want to pay the extra cost. This gives needed flexibility to the act.
The general stabilization programs undertaken by the federal government for products sold in a national market will be uniform across the country. However, by agreement with provinces and/or producers the prices may be established, as I said, higher than the 90 per cent figure if the additional funds are provided by the provinces and/or producers whether by government grants or by producer levy. None of these programs can work without proper supply management. If we give the producers the kind of program that will give them an efficient operation, they will produce things until they come out of their ears. You cannot have pork or broiler chickens or eggs or anything else coming out of your ears, unless you have to plan a market and a market for all those products. You cannot afford to give them away or, better, ask the producers to give them away. We do not do that in respect of any other commodity, whether it be food or otherwise, in this nation, to my knowledge. At least the person who produces the product is not asked to give it away.
We may be able to use some of these products in food aid programs, but we must make sure we know we have the processing facilities for them. In essence I am saying that we must know where the market is domestically, we must know where it is in the world, and we must know what the requirements are for food aid programs no matter what they be and in what part of the world. Then we produce for that. You do not produce merely in the hope that someone will give you a decent price for your commodity, because in that case you would end up as in deep trouble, as has happened with many of our producers. Some will say that we will destroy the open and free market. I would say there is an open and free market in some of these commodities for some people, but not in general for all the

primary producers, the most important part of our society. They produce the mainstay of life, food.
The bill also does some house cleaning. Wheat produced outside the Canadian Wheat Board will no longer be automatically covered under the act because it is already covered under Bill C-19. The Canadian Dairy Commission sets support prices for butter and cheese, so they will no longer receive mandatory coverage. Neither will eggs which come under the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. When this bill is passed, the list of mandatory commodities will be industrial milk and cream, corn, soybeans, oats and barley produced outside the Canadian Wheat Board area, cattle, hogs and sheep. There is also provision for any other farm commodity to be included under the act by the governor in council.
In essence, Mr. Speaker, in respect of the commodities covered under this act, no commodities really are excluded from protection. Under a clause dealing with designated commodities the legislation allows the governor in council to select a new product for stabilization if conditions warrant. There is also a provision in the bill which some of my colleagues in cabinet suggest gives the Minister of Agriculture a blank cheque to support the food producers of the nation. Never before has agriculture and its representative in the cabinet, the Minister of Agriculture, been given that authority. But I want to remind members of the House that before the Minister of Agriculture is granted that authority, there is an inter-departmental committee made up of five departments which studies all things pertaining to agriculture before a decision is made. There also are five cabinet ministers who decide on anything we do. That has been the situation for some time in cabinet. They consider the matter before any major decision is made which affects not only the agricultural producers but also the consumers in this country. Anyone who says that is not so is not stating the fact.
I think this is good, because agriculture is the largest and most important industry in the whole of Canada. One out of every three jobs in Canada depends on a healthy agricultural community. It is most important that the federal government is now probably giving more leadership than in the past, which is so important for the producers of many of these commodities which are produced not only in one province, which are consumed not only in one province, but which are consumed in the large metropolitan areas where our largest concentration of population is located in Canada, and are exported to world markets.
It is most important that we have a national program for these commodities. Some of the provinces have gone ahead on their own with insurance programs. I can tell members of this House that hardly any province which has gone ahead with some kind of program on its own has not asked me when we will get the federal legislation going so that we can work together on the programs already started. We have had lengthy discussions with the farm organizations and provincial authorities in Canada concerned with this legislation. There has been lengthy discussion interdepartmentally concerning the legislation. We have received requests lately from certain groups who wish to appear before the agricultural committee to discuss this legisla-
Agricultural Stabilization Act
tion, to seek information and to have input. Some of them already are suggesting certain amendments to this bill.
It is a far reaching bill. It is not a lengthy bill, but it is one of the most advanced that any country in the world is providing for its agricultural producers at this time. As I said before, the U.S.A., our big competitor to the south, is asking its producers to go all-out to produce everything they can for society. At the same time they are not offering one bit of security. At the present time in the United States, in some of the most productive areas of that country the farm organizations are taking up a petition not to ask their farmers to increase production but to decrease production by ten per cent. This has not happened in Canada and we do not want it to happen. We want to build confidence in the producers of agricultural products in Canada not only for the good of the producers but also for the good of our society, so that constant production of those commodities will be achieved; this is not only for the betterment of the agricultural community, and not only to guarantee that young people stay in agriculture, but also for the betterment of Canada as a whole.
So long as we have properly planned programs such as this stabilization program, it will cost the government hardly anything, if anything at all, in the long run. It will not cost the producers anything, and it will be a good form of insurance for the whole nation and for all the countries in the world which depend on Canada to supply them with a certain amount of food.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to debate Bill C-50 may I first point out that, naturally, I was very interested in the minister's remarks and in particular pleased to hear him say that interested groups would be welcome to appear before the committee when this bill is studied there. Right across this country today a great debate is taking place in the farm communities, and perhaps even in some of the larger cities, regarding farm income security, which principle is conceived in wide

Agricultural Stabilization Act
terms and generally accepted. The challenge to parliament is how to bring it about so that, as the minister said, it will not cost the government too much, it will provide farmers with security and ensure that consumers can obtain food at a reasonable cost, a concern which has been frequently voiced by consumers in the past year or so.
Therefore, I am pleased to know that this bill will be debated at length, because if a debate is going on in the country the same subject should be debated here where the people's representatives have a chance to amend this legislation or to bring in new legislation to meet the concerns of the people. The minister said that this is a great bill, with wide ramifications. I do not consider this bill to be all that great, nor does it attempt to solve many of the problems faced by the agricultural industry in Canada today. Bill C-50 amends the Agricultural Stabilization Act which came into effect some 17 years ago, back in 1957. At that time it specified the nine major commodities which would be covered by the act.
With the relatively slow rate of inflation at that time, it was felt that a ten-year period for establishing the base price of a commodity was practicable. A mandatory support level of 80 per cent was established for those commodities in 1957. It makes sense that if you cannot control inflation, legislation must be adjusted. That is what this bill proposes to do. When the minister says that the bill is a major improvement because it reduces the base period from ten years to five years, let me point out to him that it is not a major improvement but an absolute necessity. If the country's economy continues to inflate at 16 per cent or 17 per cent a year, I am not sure that the five-year period proposed in the bill is short enough.
If we could be assured of some kind of stability in the economy, I would say that five years is ample, but in view of the inflationary spiral this period should be shortened. The minister himself said that the ten-year period laid down in the act was too long and that in the last two years the program has not worked. This was apparent in the last two years. Therefore, I think the minister should reconsider the five-year period and perhaps shorten it to two years on the basis of his own figures.
I should like to make a few comments about the percentage of support which should be mandatory. As I said previously, in 1957 the act provided for mandatory support of 80 per cent. It is a well known fact today that it takes a large amount of money to produce anything in an industry as labour-intensive industry as agriculture. To cut down on the amount of labour, machinery must be purchased. It is extremely difficult to get men and women to work on farms today as they did 30 or 40 years ago, and therefore farmers are forced to use machinery to replace manpower. It is obvious that with the greater use of machinery, production and efficiency are increased.
There is a question which I should like to put to the minister. I listened closely to him when he said that 90 per cent support by the federal government was mandatory. Am I to understand that provincial support and the support of producer organizations would be on top of that? Am I to understand that the federal government will not go higher than 90 per cent?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: No, that is not so.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
I am glad to hear the minister say that assumption is wrong, otherwise I would have castigated him severely because I believe that from time to time there are commodities which because of economic and regional pressures should receive more than 90 per cent support. I would like to think that the federal government is not limited to 90 per cent. Certainly 90 per cent is the floor; however, it is only that for the mandatory commodities. What Bill C-50 is doing is reducing the mandatory commodities. It is taking wheat, butter, cheese and eggs out of the act. We started out with nine commodities and now we are left with five. So, really, when the minister says to the agricultural communities in this country that this is a revolutionary and far reaching bill, he must realize that it also narrows down the responsibility of the federal government to the agricultural industry.
We started with nine mandatory commodities and we are ending with five-four less than we had. It is all well and good for the minister to say that the commodities which are being taken out are covered in some other way, but we are actually dealing with six commodities out of the nine, not four as I mentioned, because wheat, oats and barley will be covered by Bill C-19. Does that legislation give the same 90 per cent coverage? When saying that cheese and butter are covered by the Dairy Commission, we must ask ourselves if there is any guarantee that they will cover cheese and butter. Is there any written guarantee in the Dairy Commission legislation? Some of us would like to think there is. There may be a moral obligation, but that is about all; there are no guarantees.
Consider the famous egg question. Eggs will no longer be covered by this stabilization bill. Let us consider what the minister said, quite rightly, that eggs are protected under the Farm Products Marketing Agencies Act. What kind of guarantee is there in this agency with respect to eggs? Is there as good a guarantee as in the Agricultural Stabilization Board? Here, again, I have to say no, there is not. What assistance has the Farm Products Marketing Agency received from the government? It received $100,000 to become incorporated and to start buying eggs, and that is all. What does it cost the provinces? I do not know what it costs Ontario and Quebec, the large producers in the egg business, but I know what it costs the province of Alberta. The provincial egg marketing agency in the province of Alberta started the year with a surplus of $160,000. After it had paid its dues to CEMA it was in the red by $447,000. That totals a little better than $600,000. If the Farm Products Marketing Agency had the same support as the Stabilization Board, the federal government would be picking up part of that cost.
The $600,000 which applies to Alberta was for 8 per cent of the total market. One has to ask how widely supported they were. What support did the Agricultural Stabilization Board give to the egg agency, the minister's great dream? The minister is now changing it from 80 per cent to 90 per cent. He could have increased it to 102 per cent, 120 per cent or 130 per cent in the past year if he had wanted to help the egg agencies and CEMA to operate. He did not. The floor price on eggs, in 1974, under the Agricultural Stabilization Board was 3014 cents, and that was the bare
March 5, 1975

mandatory limit of 80 per cent. The ten-year average was 38.2 cents a dozen.
The minister did not use the authority he had under the act and increase the percentage to help the egg agencies and the egg producers across Canada. He was not interested. He thought the Farm Products Marketing Agency could handle it. That agency put the bite on the egg producers. Alberta egg producers would have to charge 6'A cents per dozen on eggs alone to pay the debt to CEMA for one year's operation. That 6 lA cents per dozen is about 10 per cent of the price the producer receives for his grade A eggs. That takes most of the profit out of egg production. What percentage of eggs are breakers, and what does 6'A cents do to the price of breakers? It means something like 20 per cent.
If the minister thinks he can hoodwink anyone by suggesting that this bill has wide-ranging ramifications and that it will be the answer to agricultural problems, he is mistaken, because he could have helped the egg producers of Canada without this bill. Why didn't he; that is the question that should be asked by the egg producers across Canada if they come before the committee. They should be asking why the government was not interested in helping them in setting up the Farm Products Marketing Agency to handle poultry and eggs. The minister thinks he can divorce himself from responsibility for those commodities. In his speech this afternoon he said something about supply management being the answer. Supply management has been tried, without government help, and it did not work very well. The government, with the present minister, I suppose can enjoy some degree of popularity among farm communities, but when the truth is known about their callous disregard for our farm communities, as they demonstrated to the egg producers, they may not be quite so popular.
What is the aim of Canada in respect of agriculture? I think it is the aim of many countries to be as self-sufficient in food as possible. We discovered that in the sugar industry. We found world sugar prices rising. We had no cushion or guarantee whatsoever because we only produce about 9 per cent or 11 per cent of our sugar requirements, mainly through sugar beet in Manitoba and Alberta. I think every country attempts to become self-sufficient in agricultural production. It is one of the first things a developing country attempts to do. We must also look at the world in which we are producing food. We must ask ourselves whether we have an obligation to produce more than we need for our own requirements. If we have the ability to produce, should we encourage that production so we can get into other markets and help the many starving and less fortunate people throughout the world? I think that a country as rich in resources as Canada should proudly indicate that it is prepared to help. We should use our resources to help the world meet its food requirements.
Let us consider the present and the expected world population. I think by the year 2000 the world population will have more than doubled. However, the area required to produce food will not have increased and in fact may well have decreased with the urbanization of some areas in the United States and Canada using up valuable agricultural land. Canada should aim to be as self-suffi-
Agricultural Stabilization Act
cient as possible and make an attempt to get its products into world markets. If that responsibility is accepted, a very long and careful look at this question of supply management must be taken.
I can understand the concern of many people over the cost of agricultural products today. Huge amounts of money are needed to capitalize, to increase production and to create greater efficiency of production. I can understand the desire for income security on farms because of the amount of money borrowed, the amount of money spent and the high interest paid on debts. But I say that if we accept the obligation we must take a long look at the concept of supply management. When I consider the Agricultural Stabilization Board, some of the mandatory commodities, how well we have done and how much money we have poured into certain aspects of agriculture, I wonder whether that money has really promoted more production or whether it has had a tendency to decrease production.
One of the industries most often referred to is the dairy industry. I have the figures here to show how much money was spent to maintain it. I am not going to put them on the record, Mr. Speaker, because as a member of this House for 17 years I am ashamed of them. The money spent has not maintained the industry. A few years ago the province of Alberta was losing four dairy farmers every day, and I think that figure was pretty well representative of the whole of Canada. As legislators, we must ask ourselves why we are still losing the industry in spite of all the money that was spent on it. I do not think I have eaten Canadian butter in my own home in the past two years, Mr. Speaker; it has all been New Zealand butter.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member is aware that on the average, industrial milk producers in Canada get $2.80 per 100 pounds more than producers in the United States at the present time. Also, that there is an increase in milk production now.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not arguing about how much farmers are paid. I said I had the figures here. But we as legislators must question the manner in which the money is spent, if we are still losing the industry. What is wrong? That is what I want to know, and I hope in the debate on this bill that question will be dealt with. Why

March 5, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
have we spent so much money and yet continue to lose dairy farmers all across the country?
The minister admitted that our neighbour to the south is our main competitor in the agricultural market. They are going all-out to produce as much as they can. Just a few years ago the United States had a program which paid their farmers not to produce. They also had a land retirement program through which some 60 million acres were retired, but it is now back in extensive agricultural production. They are being encouraged to put the land back into production because that country has a balance of payments problem with regard to energy. They want to sell agricultural goods throughout the world to offset their high expenditures in energy. We must recognize that they are a keen competitor.
It is all very well for this bill to give mandatory support and have the object of farm income security, but this should not be at the expense of efficiency on the farm. I am a farmer and I know how farmers hate the word "efficiency", but I am speaking generally of the agricultural industry. I am very concerned when I hear of Australian cattle selling for eight cents, nine cents or ten cents per pound. I wish I could do something about their costs, but I cannot. We should be able to do something about costs in this country, however, to ensure that we remain competitive throughout the world.
We should be as self-sufficient in agriculture as possible, but we cannot isolate ourselves from the trading communities of the world. From time to time we may put a temporary embargo on commodities coming into Canada in order to provide some protection to the industry. For instance, strawberries should only be allowed into British Columbia after their crop is in. We should not allow dumping of agricultural commodities in this country. But we should recognize legitimate competition. If the object of this bill is to isolate our community from the rest of the world, that is a step in the wrong direction.
It is up to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to help the industry remain as competitive and as efficient as possible. When the Agricultural Stabilization Act was passed, its purpose was to shore up the industry from time to time. The nine commodities it covered were considered to be those that affected our agricultural economy; butter, cheese, eggs, wheat, hogs, sheep and cattle all had an economic effect on our various regions and, indeed, on the whole of Canada. This bill narrows the responsibility.
The minister spoke of Canada's aim. This is something which concerns me also, Mr. Speaker. Having chosen agriculture as my vocation, I am very proud of that way of life. As more and more capital is required, agriculture becomes pretty big business; and when that happens perhaps some of the zest for that way of life is lost. I think the minister's remarks on this bill should be examined. It is not good enough for him to be suddenly concerned about the potato industry.

speechtext: I used that as an example.

The minister's remarks about the price of potatoes in New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island are too little and too late. Potatoes have been around for a long time, and in the past they have been supported by the Agricultural Stabilization Board. If the minister had been

as concerned as he would have people believe, he could have given the industry support without coming to parliament. He did not have to wait. He must have known the situation because surely the figures were available. It does not take a genius to realize that if it costs $600 an acre to grow potatoes in New Brunswick and the farmer receives only $200, he cannot survive. If the government had been really concerned about the potato industry it did not need to wait for Bill C-50 to offer some help. The same thing is happening with potatoes as happened with eggs. The minister tried to put that matter in the hands of another board. Another board is not the answer. The aims of Canada and the Minister of Agriculture have to be guided. Let us consider the cattle industry. I did not particularly want to speak about that industry because I am involved in it and some people claim one becomes self-motivated when looking at one's own industry. The minister blundered about in that industry for a whole year with on again, off again subsidies.
A couple of weeks ago I asked the minister in the House for some assurance with regard to the 42 cents a hundred on beef. I asked whether that assurance was being given to the beef industry. The minister replied yes, it was. I then made the modest request that it be averaged twice a year. The minister's answer is recorded in Hansard: he said "impossible". I was so dumbfounded that I did not ask a supplementary question. I thought there must be something wrong and I would ask the question the next day. In committee, I put that suggestion to the livestock people of the minister's department. They said, "No, it is not impossible. We are averaging it every month right now." Certainly it could be done every six months. It is a question of not doing it too often and not having to make the payments too often. It is a value judgment. Being civil servants, I knew it was not their judgment as to how often would be too often, but surely the minister cannot say that every six months is too often. Some provincial ministers of agriculture would like this to be done quarterly. I have nothing against doing it quarterly. I am perhaps more generous and understanding of the minister's problems. Every six months would satisfy me and I am certain it would satisfy the agricultural industry.

speechtext: I told you we are reviewing it.

I said in this House that the minister should pay $50 a head with respect to every cow that goes to slaughter. Possibly the minister could have obtained some assistance

on that from the provincial governments. It would have been a step in the right direction. It would have removed a certain number of cows from the market. It is no good having a minister of agriculture who looks and talks like a farmer but does not have the ability to stay ahead of the agricultural industry. It is easy to criticize the minister's program and say it is too little and too late. Provincial ministers of agriculture came to Ottawa in the past year asking the federal Minister of Agriculture to show some leadership because this is a national problem.
The minister made a rather interesting speech this afternoon. He said that under Bill C-50 the program can be regionalized. I think that is good, because that has been part of the problem in the past. For example, the embargo on potatoes in the maritimes hurt the maritimes, Alberta and other parts of the country. I listened to the minister closely when he said we can regionalize. However, he said the maritimes must realize that the region will include Quebec and Ontario. speechtext:
I appreciate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) trying to defend me. I am going to end my remarks because I realize my time has nearly expired. As we look ahead there will be many challenges to face. The energy crisis caused some problems in agricultural production. Japan and Germany have ceased to take any more agricultural products than they absolutely need to feed their nations. However, we must also realize that the energy crisis that is causing problems for the industrial world is bringing money to underdeveloped countries. They will be able to buy agricultural commodities and we will be able to sell to them.
The minister said it is very difficult for the government to buy products under some kind of support program because you cannot then give them away. He said you cannot do this, and you cannot do that. I say there is no difficulty whatsoever. The government can buy all the goods it wants. There is no problem in canning meat; it has been done before. There is no problem in buying potatoes from Prince Edward Island or Alberta; it has been done before.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: What are you going to do with them?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
I just said the underdeveloped countries will have money. They will demand food. They will want a higher standard of living. The government has bought these products before. It has bought potatoes and it has bought pork. I quote from the 1973-74 annual report of the Agricultural Stabilization Board:
Quantities of board potatoes were processed into starch-
Why can the minister not do this now? Why did he not do it last December when prices were falling? I say to the minister that the underdeveloped countries will have money. Take Nigeria, for example. That little country which is almost in the centre of Africa produces as much, if not a little more, oil than Canada. It has no means of using that amount of oil. It is for sale. Nigeria is going to be wealthy, and it will be wanting food. We can produce and we can also turn off production. Farmers want to produce. That is why they go into agriculture. They want to see things grow. They want to run their hands through the soil to see what it will produce.
It is the same with livestock men; they want to see animals grow; they want to produce more animals. Don't turn the farmers off by saying, "I don't know what to do with these potatoes. I don't know what to do with these cows." The government must show some imagination. Between 1972 and 1974 the minister enjoyed a great deal of support in cabinet. Since then the hon. gentleman's popularity has declined. They do not need him now, so they are cutting down the amount in his pocketbook. He can no longer envisage great programs. He asks, "What shall we do with these potatoes?" He brings a bill before parliament and describes it as the most revolutionary legislation in the free world. Mr. Speaker, legislation will not solve the problems of the agriculture industry. Heart and desire will. The minister appears to be burdened with a great load; on some days he looks tired. Let us gear him up. We are prepared to push ideas at him and help him with his job.

Agricultural Stabilization Act

speechtext: Give us some ideas, then. I have not heard any from the hon. member.

speechtext: What he now proposes is too little and too late. Let him get on with the job and show leadership in the field of agriculture. Do not turn off production but, rather, turn on production because the underdeveloped countries are waiting for this food.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the minister opened this debate I expected to learn about some new direction the government intended to take in order to improve the position of those engaged in agriculture. However, as the previous speaker has said, this bill is completely unnecessary; it does nothing that the old bill could not do, and it contains no new ideas. It sounds very much as though the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) had drafted it. It is merely a reworking of a bunch of words. The minister and the department will have to produce new solutions to agricultural problems.
When the first bill was introduced, prices of agricultural products were relatively stable; declining levels were relatively easy to calculate and predict. That is not the situation today. The government, by one means or another, has been able effectively to eliminate all surpluses in all agricultural commodities. This afternoon the minister talked about potatoes. There is no surplus in potatoes. What has happened is that in most parts of Canada potatoes are so expensive that people are not using the quantities they used in the past. It seems to me that when potatoes are selling to the public for 79 cents for five pounds, and when the farmers in the maritimes find there is no relationship between the price they are getting and the price paid by the consumer, there is something very wrong with the whole process and that the minister should be looking at it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: What do you think we are doing?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: Well, if you are looking at it, it is not being reflected in legislation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: The hon. member knows as well as I do that there is legislation on the books.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: I wish the minister had made his speech when he had the opportunity.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: You were not listening.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has not made a speech for a long time, and the agricultural economy has changed drastically since I last heard him. I expected him to say something about these problems. If the minister wanted to pay a subsidy to farmers in the maritimes who are producing potatoes, all he had to do was pay it; the legislation providing for subsidies is wide open.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: We did it for seven years.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Certainly it was done for a number of years. But why does the hon. gentleman not have the guts to do it now? Why must he wait until farmers are destroying potatoes which ought to be going to feed consumers who need them either in the domestic market or elsewhere?

The minister talks about an arrangement between Ontario, Quebec and the western provinces. In other words, he is not talking about regionalization at all. Regionalization implies dealing with the area in which the problem has arisen. This is what the minister should be doing, and he has not done it.
Frankly, this amendment to the stabilization legislation is not needed. The Agricultural Stabilization Act set no ceiling, no limits. The governor in council could put any price under potatoes he wished as long as it did not fall below the 80 per cent level on a ten-year average. The minister cannot say he was unable to make changes. He may not at present have the staff to enable him to do it, but it is certainly not because the act fails to provide him with the necessary authority.
We gather from the minister that he has unlimited access to the financial resources of the country, not subject to the control exercised by five of his senior cabinet colleagues. In that case, why does he not take action? It is not difficult to set a fair price. The minister could set the price for potatoes at 10 cents per pound; he would not find any flood coming back from other parts of Canada.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: Check the storage in Quebec, Ontario and the maritimes. It was about 40 per cent up, compared with last year.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
The minister says he has checked the storage in the maritimes and Quebec and that there is a large quantity of potatoes in store. He says there is a surplus. In that case, the surplus is not only in the maritimes; it is in the rest of the country as well. This does not mean he cannot put a decent price on potatoes. It does not mean the potatoes have to be fed to the pigs, as we did during the depression. People are paying high prices for potatoes in the stores.
Farm problems become compounded when there is a surplus and when the minister is unwilling to impose controls. Subsidizing the production of some commodities does not always solve problems. Let me refer to three commodities which were very much to the fore in days gone by-butter, skim milk and sugar beets. Sure we had problems with those commodities, and sure we solved those problems. How, Mr. Speaker? We discouraged production. Now there is a shortage of skim milk powder. Looking ahead, it is easy to foresee that not enough fluid milk will be produced in this country unless farmers are given some assurance that markets will be stable.
Today, the farmer is a specialist. In the old days he was content if he planted four or five acres to potatoes, to sugar beets, turnips and other crops. He grew his own corn, kept some beef cattle on the property, and about 500 hens. If he encountered problems, they had to do with only one or two commodities. What has happened? We established quotas and drove small butter producers out of business. At one time there were many farmers in Quebec. Ten or 15 years ago, in my area, there were 1,400 farmers; now, about 400 work about three-quarters of the original land. They work harder than ever and make less money than ever.
March 5, 1975

The other day I talked to a relatively prosperous farmer in my area who runs a farm operation worth between a quarter and half a million dollars. He said that he made more money from the interest on his bank deposits than from his farm operation last year. He made less than $10,000 from his farm. If we want to lend young farmers $150,000 as an inducement to take up farming, we must create the kind of climate in which farmers can make a living and pay the money back.
Also, we have a responsibility to consumers. We must make sure that farmers produce all the commodities which consumers use, and in sufficient quantity. Only if we give guarantees will farmers stay in business and produce food. What has been happening, Mr. Speaker? In Ontario not enough of certain commodities is being produced. For example, fluid milk production is down. It is possible that not quite enough is being produced. Not enough cheese is being produced and not enough butter. Oh, yes, we can stabilize production of these commodities, but at some cost. You stabilize markets by creating shortages. The Canadian Dairy Commission paid out, in the period 197374, about $143 million for industrial milk production. That is how much it cost us to stabilize a market.
The minister must know which commodities need stabilizing, which need designating and what are the problems in agriculture. Price, as well, can be designated. I do not think Canadians have complained about necessary farm subsidies. All the same, I do not think the minister has met his responsibilities adequately. Consider what has happened to cattle. Farmers listened to the government and slaughtered low grade cattle; the government provided a subsidy for top category cattle. Clearly, the cattle business needs help. The governments of Ontario, Quebec and the western provinces subsidized the cow-calf operator because he was the weak link in the beef production chain. Despite this help, the price of day-old calves dropped from a high, two years ago, of between $67 and $70 to a low of $2 and $3. This happened in my area. Although the provinces and the minister wanted to help the cattle industry, they did not do enough to help the cow-calf operator.
Perhaps the minister does not really understand agriculture; perhaps he only knows how to grow corn and soybeans. In any event, his attempts at stabilizing production have not always helped. In the case of eggs, government intervention was not helpful in the least. But one thing is clear: if you want agriculture to continue, you must give people incentives to stay in the agricultural business. Today our farmers, on average, are reaching the age of retirement. Most of them are over 50. Unless we entice young people into agriculture, it does not matter very much what we do about the price structure. What difference does a price structure make if you cannot induce people to take up an occupation in which they must work sometimes seven days a week for unlimited hours? If young people do not want to take on the job, there will not be an agricultural industry in this country's future.
Farmers are mors necessary than ever, because so-called industrialized farms do not work. Some time ago one heard a great deal of talk about vertically integrated farm operations or corporate farms which many thought would be a great success because of their supposed access to
Agricultural Stabilization Act
markets. Well, the experiment was tried and found to be not successful. My hon. friends from Quebec know of the experiment in the broiler industry. Farm corporations hired farms and farmers to look after the hens, gave them 10 cents per bird and supplied all the money for the operation. The farmer had to supervise the operation. The corporations rented the buildings, paid for the feed, bore all costs and were responsible for marketing. But, Mr. Speaker, such farm corporations time after time have gone broke. Clearly, farming does not lend itself to vertical integration. That is the case not only in this country but in other countries such as Russia where corporate farming does not work. You cannot run a farm on an eight-hour day. When the sun shines, you make hay, and when it rains-

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Perhaps you whitewash the barn or you do something else. With government intervention in agriculture today, requiring income tax forms, farm reports, unemployment insurance payments, compensation payments and all the other things, the farmer has to spend all his rainy days doing the necessary bookkeeping rather than taking it easy. In any event, there has not been much success in corporate farming in this country or in other countries such as Russia, but that appears to be the direction in which the minister is moving. I suggest the alternative is simple. We must help young people to get into the agricultural industry, and to do that we must have stabilization of prices.
What is wrong with stabilized prices? What is wrong with the formula we used before? In the past we took 80 per cent of the ten-year average as the prescribed price for given commodities. Inflation has had its effect on this ten-year average and there is absolutely no relationship between the input costs to produce a farm commodity ten years ago and the input cost of producing that commodity today. Let me give an example. If you were feeding poultry ten years ago, you were probably buying feed concentrates at $35 or $37 a ton. Today the cost could be anywhere from $200 to $300 a ton. So there is no relationship. And, of course, we do not have indexing. This should not be accepted as an excuse for the government's inaction in respect of the use of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Perhaps at the time this act was adopted the members were smart in that they did not put in a ceiling. When you stabilize things there is no need for a ceiling. This is within the minister's discretion and he can take into account the increase in input costs and the fact that the use of fertilizer has become more necessary and it is more expensive. It is very necessary to use fertilizer in order to produce on farms that have been in production for a long time.
We must develop a program to provide reasonably stable prices. I do not believe it is acceptable across the country to have the potato producers in the maritimes or in Ontario selling their product at such a loss that they will not be able to buy fertilizer for their crops next year. In fact, if there is any danger of a large portion of the potato

March 5, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
crop being lost this year, many of those growers will not be able to buy the gasoline necessary next year to operate the equipment required to put in the crop.
I suggest that would not be in my interest, certainly not in the interest of the producers and, more importantly, not in the interest of the Canadian public. We will all depend on the production of potatoes next year, the year after and the year after that. If these producers leave the farm, they probably will not return. I do not see any evidence to indicate that this government realizes that in order to keep the young people in agricultural production, they will require a great deal of assistance. Unless we keep these people on the farms we will have shortages of potatoes and many other agricultural commodities.
It is a national disaster to have energy resources limited, because we will not be able to enjoy the kind of life we have enjoyed in the past. This is a very unfortunate situation and I am sure everyone will lament the end of a period of energy abundance. This does not have to be the case in respect of agricultural production because these commodities are renewable. We can increase production as long as we are willing to stabilize profits. Before the end of this debate I would like the minister to tell us why he has done nothing about the present problems in respect of potato production or the cow-calf operation. Why has he not done something about these situations?
From my understanding and experience, there is very little the minister cannot do to help the agricultural industry. I am not suggesting that he should take measures that will result in cutting off commodities from the United States, but any minister of agriculture who allows commodities to be dumped across the border into Canada at a lower price, or even at a competitive price, is not doing his job. The Minister of Agriculture should not allow another country to use Canada as a surplus warehouse for potatoes, tomatoes, root crops or anything else. As long as the minister allows that to happen, he is failing this nation which depends on our agricultural industry as a cheap source of food. Our industry has always provided Canadians with food at reasonable prices and the industry is still doing this.

speechtext:
I suppose it depends on what you are talking about, as there are many prices for concentrates. I was not really being specific; I was just trying to draw a comparison between input costs over the last ten years. If the

minister says that concentrates sell for $110 a ton, and will agree that they used to sell at $10, $15 or $20 a ton, that is all right with me. The minister apparently missed the point I was trying to make, so I had better say it again. Input costs have gone up out of proportion to the price of the commodity whatever it may be. If you take 80 per cent of the ten-year average, you are relating it to the selling price of the commodity but the input costs are not really taken into account.
This bill does have a clause for indexing, but that indexing is not tied to input or anything else. It seems to me that all it is saying is that there will be an indexing aspect, but even without that indexing clause the minister still has the right to stabilize prices. There was never any doubt that he could set the price of a particular commodity. We had a floor, but there was no ceiling on it. We could have continued to subsidize as high as necessary. That was a judgment the Stabilization Board made concerning the level. Over the years many commodities have been subsidized. We might look at the list which appears in the annual report. We find, for instance, that potatoes were subsidized. The report reads:
Order in Council P.C. 1972-8 of January 18, 1972, authorized the board to purchase a minimum of 200 hundredweight and a maximum of 1,333 hundredweight of Canada No. 1 grade potatoes from individual producers. Initial payment on acceptance of the board's offer to purchase was to be 75 cents per hundredweight to each eligible producer, plus an additional 75 cents per hundredweight on delivery to the board of all potatoes purchased by the board from the producer. Quantities of board potatoes were processed into starch, or fed to livestock, and the total expenditure in 1973-74, exclusive of the principal amounts paid in the 1971-72 and 1972-73 fiscal years was $35,927.
The subsidization was l'/2 cents. That does not seem to me to be any great bargain. I presume that because there was no particular fuss last year, it was a help; but it cost the Canadian public $35,000. If we could reduce the price of potatoes in the store by 20 cents on a ten-pound bag, we could pay the producer an extra three cents. It really does not make any difference to the consumer whether he pays it in the form of a tax or over the counter.
I do not believe we have done anything to solve these problems as they have developed. We have been too generous with our friends south of the border who have caused this country immense difficulty for many years. Now, in looking at GATT, it would seem that it is time we gave a new definition to "dumping" in this country. It has always been held that if hot-house tomatoes sell for 69 cents a tube, and tomatoes come in from the United States or Mexico, from the field, at a price in keeping with their own price and below our price, no assistance could be provided. So the stabilization bill over the years did provide assistance in this field. I think most members will support this bill. I believe it should be kept in mind, however, that in reducing the ten-year period to five years, if we cannot in some way compensate, by indexing for the rise in input costs to the farmer, and cannot bring that into relationship with the price he receives in the particular year for his commodity and use that as an index so we will be in a much better position to decide what is a fair price to the farmer and decide on it in conjunction with the farmer, we will not have the kind of stability we want.

The five-year average has not solved this problem. My impression is that indexing will not solve it. In effect, in respect of this bill we are agreeing that although we set a floor price there is in fact no mandatory floor price established for any commodities that are outside the designated commodities, and there is a floor price only for those designated commodities when they meet the requirements of the five-year average. That is totally out of line. It does not take into consideration the escalation of costs. It would appear to me that there is no way that the index, which is not spelled out in the legislation, can apply to that five-year average so as to create a solution to the problem I have indicated. If we look over the period in which the Stabilization Board has been in operation, and consider the fact that in those years we have paid roughly $1 Vi billion for the subsidization of agricultural commodities, and if we apply that to the assistance that has been provided to the individual from that payment, we will find it has been responsible to a large extent for keeping many of our farmers in production and has made it possible for them to continue in a viable industry.
It is interesting to look at what some of these products have been. The major one, of course, has been milk, mostly butter products. The amount in that case is $136 million. The amount in respect of skim milk is $15 million. In respect of milk for manufacturing the amount is $154 million, and for cream for manufacturing the amount is $83 million. Other products we have supported over the years received amounts considerably less that the amounts for that industry. These involved such things as hogs, in respect of which we paid $92 million so that the producers would remain in the hog production industry in this country. It is much easier to get into this type of production than it is to get out of it.
We have assisted producers in respect of lamb, wool and potatoes over a period of 16 years by paying almost $9 million to stabilize the prices. Here is an interesting one: we paid $38,805,119 to stabilize the sugar beet industry, yet this government allowed the closing of all the sugar beet factories in Ontario. While the government embarked on an open market sugar policy, it made it possible for only a few sugar beet plants to exist in Manitoba. This is a field in which we would have been able to provide a buttress against the world price of sugar. I am surprised that some friends of the minister did not tell him this when the industry closed in Ontario, because we were in a position where we could have produced, had we had the factories, probably 50 per cent of our own sugar without much difficulty.
In my opinion, this legislation has been a valuable asset to Canadian farmers. I also believe it has been a valuable asset to the consumers of Canada. It has enabled the government to provide assistance to agriculture in this country. Farmers have not become rich on any agricultural commodity in this country, not even on soybeans. Many times they have had to give up making payments on their farms so that they could provide Canadians with a cheap product. When things became really desperate we assisted them, but only in a very small measure, through the stabilization act.
Agricultural Stabilization Act
My criticism of both the old act and this bill is that it is left entirely up to the Minister who administers the act to decide whether or not an order in council will be passed, and whether it will be passed soon enough to be of assistance to farmers. Right now there are many young farmers who cannot make payments on their farms because they cannot sell their calves at a price that will carry the cost of the operation. I am sure that many producers of potatoes in the maritimes which sell at 1.5 cents per pound are not able to carry their production costs and therefore are not able to make their payments. These are two agricultural products on which the minister could ask for an order in council in cabinet tomorrow.
Under the act some things are prohibited, but the minister is certainly not prohibited from designating any commodity that he wants to designate, and set any price he thinks is appropriate. Another thing that has never been impossible to do is for this House to pass support legislation for agriculture, because all consumers in this country know very well that farming is a marginal operation which brings marginal returns, yet it has been providing consumers with food of a very high calibre, often at unreasonably low cost.
In closing, I would say that the minister should make the speech at the end of this debate that he neglected to make at the beginning. I have defended this minister day in and day out to farmers in my constituency. I say that as Minister of Agriculture he is responsible to farmers, and he is excercising this responsibility. But I say that responsibility to consumers belongs to another minister. Yet farmers ask me why, if the minister is responsible for looking after them, they are in such bad shape. I say this is a question that only the minister can answer. This bill would have allowed him to do many things which he has not taken the opportunity to do.
