speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always quite interesting to follow a debate dealing with problems in our farming industry. During the past few years, some strange things have been said on the condition of farmers. I remember among others that a former minister of agriculture had stated that a farmer merely needed four cows and two sows to realize a net income of $2,000 yearly. The minister was not re-elected, because nobody took his word. It is really absurd to say such things.
In my opinion, if it were so easy there would be no marketing problems for farm products. The problem highlighted during consideration of Bill C-50 has existed for many years. We are beating about the bush. We are looking for solutions and when they are found to be inefficient, they are altered and we then say that we will try over again if necessary.
This reminds of the day when, in the Standing Committee on Agriculture, the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) as a member of parliament, reminded the former minister of agriculture of a few things and asked him whether the alternative formula had been drawn up by economists or other civil servants. He added that economists have a gift for making us try a formula, of getting us down in the hole and then dropping us in it, but

March 5, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
that they do not produce formulas allowing you to come out of it.
How true! Even today. To wit, the many studies made in Canada, by the provinces, commissions of all sorts, on farming problems. Reports have been tabled, studied; laws have been passed but the problem remains the same because we do not delve into the basic issues.
This is so true, Mr. Speaker, that during the 1957-58 session, at which time I myself was active as a farmer, we had marketing problems, if not total chaos, and we could not make up from the sale of our products our production costs, let alone make profits.
An election was held at that time. A program was submitted to the electorate by a party which assured us that legislation would be passed to stabilize farm incomes, farm product prices. We were quite happy. We followed closely the debate that took place in this House. It was a debate on the Agricultural Stabilization Act, Chapter A-9, that could be summed up as follows:
Considering the advisability of enacting provisions in order to stabilize farm product prices to help the agricultural industry get a fair return on its work and its investment, as well as to maintain a fair balance between prices received by farmers and the cost of commodities and services they buy, that is what will provide farmers with a fair share of the national income. It was the way I just quoted during the 1957-58 session.
We are now in 1975 and working to amend that act which did not give the results we had hoped for; we are now patching it up, and trying to amend it in the following way:
His Excellency the Governor General has recommended to the House of Commons the present measure to amend the Agricultural Stabilization Act to amend in the manner prescribed the definition "agricultural commodity";
An agricultural commodity is not difficult to define. It includes all commodities produced by farmers, by agricultural producers. There are many of them, and I think all producers need to have some protection so as to be assured an income from that operation.
It goes on to say, and I quote:
to shorten from ten to five years the period from which the base price for each agricultural commodity is determined, and to alter in the manner prescribed the method of establishing the prescribed price in relation to a named commodity and in relation to a designated commodity;
I quite agree on setting up a period, I quite agree on shortening this study, because it would only be fair to the producers of today, to do away with the five years of starvation and low prices. Keeping this in the Act would not be fair to them.
In fact, what I find quite surprising is this: to enable the Board to exercise powers for the purpose of stabilizing the price of an agricultural commodity; under the circumstances prescribed to empower the Board to enter into agreements with provinces and/or producers to provide for a greater prescribed price that would otherwise apply and, for any increased costs to be borne by the province and/or producers;
I am somewhat surprised at finding that this board will determine prices on the basis of these factors. Will all

relevant factors actually enter into the calculation of production costs, and will this calculation be done by people who really possess the skill required and who will be able to submit figures which will not have to be reduced later by a given percentage, to conform with a price set beforehand and which would not be fair to the producers.
This is another factor on which the minister will have to provide much explanation when the bill is studied in committee, if we are to improve the present legislation, make it more efficient and more generous for producers, without neglecting consumers. We must have justice for everyone. But the purpose of the bill is first to protect farm producers.
The recommendation goes further when it says that the governor in council will be able to establish-
... ceilings on the quantity or value of an agricultural commodity eligible for price stabilization; and to provide for consequential
matters.
Mr. Speaker, I am prepared to believe that it is necessary to determine the quality of agricultural commodities, to meet adequately consumers' needs. But I do not agree on a few points. Nowhere in this bill is it provided that this provision will also apply to imported products.
Again recently in the province of Quebec, and perhaps this happened also elsewhere, 1 don't know, we heard about poultry producers setting their own quotas and limiting their production. A few days ago they lowered their production quotas to meet the demand, the needs on the domestic market, and to maintain price stabilization just so they would make decent profits.
But they have been fooled. There are some people who have taken the liberty of importing similar products which come from our neighbours and are marketed in our country. This has resulted-and I hope this situation will be rectified before it is too late-in disrupted production. Our producers went ahead and barbecued their chickens in the street as a mark of protest. This has been a waste of food at a time when there are needs unsatisfied in many homes of our country and elsewhere. This we term disorder. And I take the opportunity of recommending to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) an amendment he might incorporate into the bill.
One cannot be too cautious. If we want the Minister of Agriculture and the Agricultural Stabilization Board to be in a position to operate and get results, they must have the tools, they must have teeth, to enable them to dig on whenever appropriate. I have already suggested to this House-and I think several members agree with me, that since the Minister of Agriculture is responsible for food production-he should see to it that food supplies are adequate to meet the needs of the whole population. He should also be allowed to exercise control over the importation and exportation of the products we might need. At the present time, another minister is exercising this control, although he does not have as many responsibilities in this field as the Minister of Agriculture has-

speechtext: He is not taking them.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Joliette says that he is not taking them. I am inclined to believe him, because when a question was put to him in

the House this week on this subject, he said he would look into it and report later.
Mr. Speaker, I want to believe that the ministers do not have to remember everything and be able to give point-blank answers to all the questions they might be asked. I understand that very well. But to such important questions as the one he was asked, I think a minister has the obligation to give the House a more satisfactory answer.
Mr. Speaker, in connection with the 1958 Act, section 2 did define the commodities covered by the legislation. Maple syrup had not been included. Well, Mr. Speaker, this is another suggestion I am making to the minister, in order that maple syrup, a natural produce, be included under the new legislation.
Several hon. members are aware that maple syrup producers now have serious difficulties. Many have not been able to get paid for their 1973 crop. Many have not been paid for the 1974 crop either and the 1975 crop is coming. These are agricultural producers whoinvested money but did not get any return. They are in a bad situation.
I understand that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) made an effort-and I thank him-to come to an agreement between his department and the Maple Syrup Producers Association, under which financial institutions can make cash advances to enable these people to stay in business. However, since the market situation is not excellent, as I could see, financial institutions did not accept to go along with the program and nobody could get money for these products.
The hon. member for Laval (Mr. Roy) motions that it is not true. If I am mistaken I would be pleased to know it and if the situation is better, I will withdraw my words with pleasure. I am honest enough to do this.
I am told that there is now an agreement between Quebec and Ottawa for the purchase of these products. I hope that this time it well prove operative and that producers will be able to get their money as quickly as possible for their production. We shall see afterwards how to dispose of it because, after all, we are talking about sugar. With white sugar at 75 cents a pound, at least we should not have to pay that price for our own sugar- maple sugar-and it should be possible for us to find buyers here with a little promotion in all the provinces.
There is another matter with which I would also want to deal, that of middlemen. I am quite upset Mr. Speaker. As soon as an increase in the price of an agricultural product is announced, newspapers immediately print in large headlines that it is scandalous, as it has just happened in the province of Quebec. In February, Quebec's Agricultural Marketing Board decreed that whole milk would be sold 51 cents a quart as from March 1. There was a general outcry.
The public, the consumers were led to believe that they would be gouged mostly by those wicked producers, those bad farmers. There is a total lack of information. Education is needed in that regard.
Mr. Speaker, last weekend, I had the opportunity of meeting a group of farmers' wives and they asked me a question. Of course, those ladies are interested in the
Agricultural Stabilization Act
operation but are not necessarily involved in the production. They wanted to know why milk was selling at 51 cents a quart. I told them that, well, it was because we had to support diary farmers if we wanted to have milk to drink. If the producers get no money, they will quit. After they have gone out of business, we shall have to buy milk somewhere else and then pay $1 a quart. Would the situation be any better? I worked out this calculation for them: 51 cents a quart, 40 quarts per hundredweight, that puts the price per hundredweight at $20.40. I asked them: Can you tell me how much of the $20.40 goes to the producer? They did not know that he gets less than $12 per hundredweight. They were not aware of that. Who is pocketing the difference?
Another point: 8 oz. softdrink bottles cost a quarter each. Take 5 bottles to get a quart or 40 ounces and you get a cost of $1.25 per quart, or $50 per hundredweight. They only ingredients are water, sugar and colouring additives. There are no complaints about that. People pay $50 per hundredweight for those drinks. They buy them, but they no longer buy fluid milk at $12, Mr. Speaker.
It can therefore be taken for granted that the Food Prices Review Board will have plenty of work to do, not only with regard to farmers, but also with respect to groceries and shopping centres in order to check the quality and price of other commodities, make comparisons and check whether imported products which compete with Canadian products really are of the same quality and at the same price, and if they help save anything. That would be a fine assignment for the Plumptre Commission, and an efficient, meaningful task.
Mr. Speaker, a few amendments should be made to this bill. We shall certainly discuss them when it is studied in committee, but I should like first, since this is a matter of urgent necessity, to ask the Minister of Agriculture for some information dealing with the Commission appointed to inquire into beef and veal marketing. I wish we could get a report before the year 2000, because it is getting urgent.
The present situation is disastrous: consumers probably pay less for beef, but how much do producers get as compared to last year?
I would like to back my remarks with strong arguments showing that producers, even if sometimes people accuse them of being bleeding hearts, do sometimes have reasons to complain, and that can be proven by comparing the following two stages: February 1974 and February 1975 with respect to the cost of beef as reported in La Terre de Chez Nous. For instance, a bull sold for $36.50 in February 1974 and only $19.25 in February of this year. Has there been an equivalent reduction at Steinberg's and Dominion. I would not think so. Anyway, price have sunk down by approximately that amount for the producers.
Take, for instance, the No. 3 cow: in 1974, it was sold for $38.75 a hundred, and in 1975, $18.75 a hundred, that is $20 less. The difference is substantial. Did feed grain prices change during the same period? The answer is also important. Well, in 1974, the price of barley in Montreal was $5.67 a hundred, and oats, $5.46. In February 1975, it rose to $6.26 a hundred for barley and $6.17 for oats. Production costs go up while the sales price goes down. As a result, the difference between the cost of production and the cost
3824

March 5, 1975
Agricultural Stabilization Act
price widens continually. No wonder our young people do not want to become farmers.
We have also seen a shocking increase in the price of farm machinery, and a commission, the Barber Commission, conducted an inquiry in that field. It did an excellent job, and if its report is to be implemented, there must be an agreement between the Canadian government and the other countries where our farm machinery imports are manufactured. And nothing is happening there either. The recommendations in the Barber report are not being implemented, and companies make fabulous profits at the expense of the buyers, our Canadian farmers. For this reason, things are getting worse instead of getting better.
Another area of tremendous interest to Canadian producers is that of fertilizers. What should be done? We were taught to use fertilizers. Our agronomists, after tests made in experimental farms, taught us their use. Of course, they work, they promote growth. But we are now realizing that the chemicals we are now buying at unreasonable cost are harmful to men, because they pollute the water that goes into our rivers. Our cattle have to drink that water, they graze on fast-growing grass through the use of fertilizers. This gets into their flesh, into the milk of cows, and affects human health. But that is not the problem we face today. The problem is that fertilizers are so expensive this year that many farmers will not be buying enough in proportion to their acreage. I fear a decrease in the production of feed grain. And if this happens, it is possible that next fall, more herds will disappear. Mr. Speaker, this is a serious matter. A number of producers are killing their calves. They do not keep them more than an hour. That production will not be in the market next fall. The situation is far from brilliant for those people. They do not know whether they must breed them or not, because they are not ensured a price which will allow them some return. I know what I am talking about. I do visit farms, and I am not afraid or ashamed of doing so. So I know what happens. It is for that reason that I ask the minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to urge the Commission to inquire into beef and veal marketing. We must not wait until the amendments to the agricultural stabilization board are effective. We must act now. Tomorrow, it may be too late.
There is another area on which I would like us to be on the watch and to look closely: In the course of the hearings of the special committee on egg marketing, Mr. Speaker, we examined very closely the matter of production costs. We heard many witnesses who showed us with figures what is the real production cost of a dozen of eggs. We have also heard the representatives of the Consumers' Association of Canada who showed us that they cannot afford to pay more for the eggs they have to buy for their family. But there is another "gimmick" between consumers and producers, and I would like us to examine this "gimmick", this sanctuary, in order to find out what happens in there.
I am not talking about the small retailer or the corner grocer, absolutely not. He is not the one who sets the prices; he has no authority to do so. He must pay what he is charged, and since he has paid, he wants to make a reasonable profit. It is the powerful, those we do not see,

the big companies, the magnates, and all those who know all the tricks to take over the production, store it, control it and market it at prices that they have set. Not many of these companies have gone bankrupt, but many small ones do go bankrupt. Why? Because small undertakings are powerless, because they must submit to the cartel set up by the big companies.
If we really want to go to the bottom of things, Mr. Speaker, I believe we should really have an independent body with as much courage as Mr. Justice Robert Cliche in Quebec. There is a courageous man, apparently he is doing his duty, and I congratulate him for it. I wish there were at the national level a commission with that kind of courage, headed by a chairman with the same courage, to go to the bottom of things, to tell the consumers that it is not the farm producers who are guilty if the price of food products keeps going up, and to point out to them the true culprit so that the consumers and the producers could come to an understanding and support a government which would bring law and order in this area and which would be ready to face up to the situation.
Unfortunately, we often are under the impression that our governments are weak when faced with the strong and strong when faced with the weak and it should be the opposite. We should have courageous governments who are strong when faced with the strong and who would treat them as equal. Governments should say: You are strong; I am strong because of democracy, because I have been elected, because I have been chosen to play such a role and be understanding for the weak, the low income families, the poor, those who are defenseless. If a government were understanding, if it helped those people, no one would complain.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding my remarks I hope that the Minister of Agriculture understood at least the two amendments I would like to be made to Bill C-50. I do not want to be critical; on the contrary, I do it to make my contribution so that the bill may be more comprehensive, that the legislation may be more efficient and that civil servants may get the tools needed to function and achieve the mission we wish to give them under this legislation. I shall come back to this matter in due time when we shall review it in committee. I hope that once we have reviewed this legislation together, suggested ideas to improve it and accomplished our duty, we shall be able to expect more efficiency from this legislation so that producers may be finally satisfied. Consumers will know at last to whom they pay and why they pay.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my farmers tell me that there is no question that this bill is an important step in the right direction. There are three provisions that constitute a particular improvement: first, shortening the base period on which support is calculated from ten years to five years; second, increasing from 80 to 90 per cent the percentage of the base prices which will be guaranteed; third, indexing the support levels to reflect changes in production costs. Perhaps the most promising aspect of this legislation, however, is that provision which provides for the development of federal-provincial agreements to co-ordinate the federal programs in this area with provincial programs and which anticipates the de-
March 5, 1975

velopment of programs with joint federal, provincial and producer participation.
More and more provinces have been developing their own farm stabilization measures. There is a growing need for someone to step in an co-ordinate these activities. British Columbia has an income stabilization plan in operation; Saskatchewan is planning to extend its grain stabilization scheme; Quebec seems to be considering a major project to guarantee the income of milk producers. The amendments in this bill will make it possible for the federal government to co-ordinate and integrate its measures with these provincial programs into a package, with maximum effectiveness. By providing for programs with producer participation, these amendments will make it possible for producers to be involved in stabilizing their own industry. This, too, is a step in the right direction.
I represent a constituency which produces one of the widest varieties of agricultural products in this country. To keep in close contact with those of my constituents in agriculture, after I was elected I set up an agricultural advisory committee with 14 members who, together, represent all the different types of farms in Wellington constituency and cover the whole area geographically. I would like to acquaint this House with my advisory group to show how members can maintain close contact with the farmers and, therefore, assess how valuable this legislation will be to them. The chairman of my committee is a young farmer, a recent graduate of the Ontario Agricultural College of the University of Guelph, who farms 600 acres in Guelph township. Petter Hannam, of R.R.2,

I have made sure that all these people have received copies of the bill we are considering. The feedback I get convinces me they are in favour of this kind of measure. I think it is important to ask the people who are directly concerned what they think. I am confident the farming community will welcome this measure.
A bill which improves farm stabilization policy is also of benefit to consumers. The food industry is of key importance not only to farmers but to all consumers. Measures such as this improve the reliability and efficiency of Canada's long-term food supply. They moderate the sudden fluctuations in the market which can lead to alternate shortages and surpluses, and in so doing they ensure a stable and growing Canadian food industry. This benefits all Canadians and protects them from actions such as have been taken with respect to oil and sugar, where we rely on imports to supply our markets.
Last fall, the United States undersecretary for agriculture spoke to a group of Canadian farmers in Hespeler, Ontario. He outlined his own country's plans to set aside a $10 billion fund to bail out American farmers. There is no way in which we can compete with this, but the American proposal underlines the need to look after our own producers who could be swamped by surpluses from across the border. The egg and beef producers have already been faced with this situation. More than ever before, we must work hard and quickly to maintain a strong agricultural industry in Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-50 I can only call it a disaster bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext: Oh!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FOR DEFINITION OF AGRICULTURAL COMMODITY AND BASE PRICE
speechtext:
I hear members on the other side saying "Oh!" But it was brought in years ago as an insurance for the farmers. It has served as disaster insurance. Take the bill the minister is bringing in now and compare it with the bill he is amending; you will find there is very little difference. The main difference is that he is reducing the ten years to five years, and taking the 80 per cent and bringing it up to 90 per cent. This is not even in the class of being what stability is all about in this day and age.
It would not be so bad if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) had not been stomping the country telling farmers he was going to bring in a stabilization plan which would mean stability for farmers. This legislation does not begin to compare with what some of the provinces are doing. We went to the agricultural congress in 1969 and again in 1970. The congress was called by the government because the farmers were saying the government had no agricultural policy. The farmers are still saying it. The main theme of those meetings was the need for stability in the industry. This government has done absolutely nothing to bring about stability. Now we find that the tired old stabilization plan is being amended. The farmers are being asked to accept it as a plan for bringing about stability.

At one time farming in Canada used to be a way of life. There was a much greater percentage of people on farms in previous years than now; in the neighbourhood of 30 per cent of our population was in farming. That percentage has been dwindling, until now less than 10 per cent of our people are on the farm. One of the reasons people are turning away from farming is that it is hard to make a go of farming; it is hard to make a go of that way of life. So now the people who are left on the farms are dedicated to farming and we find that they are in upper age brackets. This cannot go on. We must make an effort to bring young people into farming and replace older farmers, because older farmers just cannot go on forever.
The farmer of today is established, organized, knowledgeable, and he wants to produce. Not only does he want to produce; he can produce. The Minister of Agriculture was going around the country saying to farmers, "Produce all you can." They did. Then he went to the horticultural council and said that potato growers in New Brunswick are in trouble because they produced too much. He has spoken on many occasions about stabilization, but in many ways he has done absolutely nothing to bring about stability in the price of commodities farmers produce. He compared this year's New Brunswick Farm production with last year's. I do not think this year's was much above average.
Farmers in Canada are nervous about producing surpluses. They are nervous because of the ups and downs which have been experienced in agriculture over the years. They do not particularly want to carry on agricultural operations which are subject to these kinds of ups and downs. They see others in Canada insulating themselves against inflation. Others belong to unions, and have bargaining agents, which help them to insulate themselves.
Farmers can see that the buyers of their produce are few in number; their power is concentrated in very few hands. They know who sells most of their produce to the consumer chain stores. They know, for instance, that in the fruit and vegetable industry buying power is concentrated in the hands of about seven buyers in North America, not just in Canada. They know that their produce is handled by large organizations which deal with chain stores. They know that we have had a policy of cheap food in the past in Canada. They also know that the consumer can buy more food with one hour's work than ever before. They know they are consumers themselves; they must buy many things both for their farm organizations and to feed themselves and their families.
But, Mr. Speaker, the new generation of farmers today is not in farming for a way of life. They want some stability in their operations. This is the message they have tried to get through for some time to this government. They are not too interested in the old ways with their ups and downs, ways in which an "up" lasted maybe for two good years and a "down" for quite a few more years. After the agricultural congress was held, we experienced a couple of pretty fair years in the farming industry. But farmers are nervous: they do not feel that this is going to continue. They know the people of Canada are concerned about the loss of land from agriculture. They know there is talk of
March 5, 1975

land freezes and that in some provinces agricultural land has been frozen. They know the people of Canada like the idea of green belts and do not want everything paved over in Canada, especially in those areas where people are concentrated, usually where conditions are good for the growing of fruits, vegetables and other kinds of foods.
The Minister of Agriculture has gone stomping around Canada taking credit for all the good things which have happened in agriculture and saying many things farmers like to hear. But he had the opportunity to bring in
Agricultural Stabilization Act
legislation which could provide for stability and this is the bill he introduced. Look at the bill before us. I think he should be ashamed for having brought this bill before the House, for introducing it in this forum, especially after what he has been telling farmers for the last two years. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
